claim: Organisms evolving toward greater complexity were selected across aeons to use energy and resources efficiently.
source: Organisms evolving toward greater complexity were selected across aeons to use energy and resources efficiently.
evidence: This is a general statement about evolutionary principles presented in the abstract without specific experimental data but drawing on established evolutionary theory.

claim: Efficiency in organisms depended on prediction at every stage.
source: Efficiency depended on prediction at every stage: first a clock to predict the planet's statistical regularities; then a brain to predict bodily needs and compute commands that dynamically adjust the flows of energy and nutrients.
evidence: This claim is supported by the author's theoretical framework about predictive regulation discussed throughout the manuscript.

claim: Predictive regulation (allostasis) frugally matches resources to needs and forms a core principle of organismal design.
source: Predictive regulation (allostasis) frugally matches resources to needs and thus forms a core principle of our design.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the principle of allostasis that is elaborated throughout the manuscript.

claim: The steam engine converted thermal energy to work.
source: Humans, reaching a pinnacle of cognitive complexity, eventually produced a device (the steam engine) that converted thermal energy to work and were suddenly awash in resources.
evidence: This is a historical fact about the steam engine's function.

claim: Boundless consumption in many nations challenges regulatory mechanisms, causing obesity, diabetes, drug addiction and their sequelae.
source: Today boundless consumption in many nations challenges all our regulatory mechanisms, causing obesity, diabetes, drug addiction and their sequelae.
evidence: This claim connects modern consumption patterns to health outcomes, drawing on epidemiological observations.

claim: Atmospheric carbon dioxide is rising and destabilizing the climate.
source: Atmospheric carbon dioxide is rising and destabilizing the climate.
evidence: This is a well-established scientific fact about climate change.

claim: Obesity is increasing globally.
source: Obesity is increasing – although multitudes still live in extreme poverty – accompanied by increases in cases of hypertension and type 2 diabetes.
evidence: This is supported by epidemiological data and cited later in the manuscript.

claim: Addiction to opioids and other drugs is rising, resulting in more deaths from overdose.
source: Addiction to opioids and other drugs is also rising, resulting in more deaths from overdose.
evidence: This is a statement about epidemiological trends in drug addiction.

claim: Natural selection favors organisms that gather and use energy efficiently.
source: For 200,000 years we were governed by a close matching of resources to needs. We, like all our progenitors, were shaped by nature's broadest constraint: natural selection favors organisms that gather and use energy efficiently.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of evolutionary biology.

claim: Everything from proteins and cells up to organs and the behavior of whole organisms evolved to be efficient and to be efficiently regulated by an efficient brain.
source: Everything, from proteins and cells up to organs and the behavior of whole organisms, evolved to be efficient – and to be efficiently regulated by an efficient brain (Sterling and Laughlin, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sterling and Laughlin, 2015.

claim: In the past 250 years, many humans now live amidst resources that greatly exceed biological needs.
source: But then in a flash – the past 250 years – everything changed and many of us now live amidst resources that greatly exceed our biological needs.
evidence: This is a historical observation about resource availability following industrialization.

claim: The cell is an analogue computer where all information is processed by chemistry.
source: In essence, the cell is an analogue computer where all information is processed by chemistry (Bray, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bray, 2009.

claim: Prokaryotes accomplish their functions at an energy cost approaching the lower limit set by physical law.
source: Prokaryotes accomplish these functions at an energy cost approaching the lower limit set by physical law (Noor et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Noor et al., 2010.

claim: ATP transfers a fixed packet of energy of about 20 kBT in one millisecond.
source: The energy boost provided by ATP is small, about 20 kBT (where kB is the Boltzmann constant, and T is temperature) in one millisecond, and modestly exceeds the mean energy of thermal noise.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about ATP energetics based on biophysical measurements.

claim: The energy boost provided by ATP is enough to tilt a protein from 'almost certainly not active' to 'almost certainly active'.
source: Yet, because a protein molecule is continually energized by thermal noise, the energy boost provided by ATP is enough to tilt the protein from 'almost certainly not active' to 'almost certainly active' (Astumian, 1997; Astumian, 2015; Motlagh et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Astumian, 1997; Astumian, 2015; Motlagh et al., 2014.

claim: Prokaryotes produced ATP by burning sugars to drive an ATP synthase turbine embedded in the cell membrane.
source: Prokaryotes produced ATP by burning sugars to drive an extraordinary nanoscale turbine (ATP synthase) embedded in the cell membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about prokaryotic metabolism.

claim: The ATP synthase turbine spins at 9,000 rpm and each revolution produces three ATP molecules.
source: This turbine spins at 9,000 rpm, and each revolution spits out three ATP molecules (He et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to He et al., 2018.

claim: The ATP synthase turbine is 90% efficient.
source: The turbine is 90% efficient, meaning that 90% of the energy that goes into the turbine is 'captured' by ATP (Kinosita et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kinosita et al., 2000.

claim: Prokaryotes remained tiny, just a few micrometers in diameter.
source: Yet prokaryotes remained tiny – just a few micrometers in diameter.
evidence: This is an observational fact about prokaryotic cell size.

claim: Prokaryote genomes remained small and did not accumulate information.
source: Their genomes also remained small and did not accumulate information.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about prokaryotic genome evolution.

claim: When prokaryotes needed new genes to adapt to novel conditions, they were forced to shed nonessential genes.
source: They had encoded all the genes they could afford energetically, so when new genes were needed to adapt to novel conditions, cells were forced to shed their nonessential genes (Lane, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lane, 2014.

claim: The location of the power plant in the cell membrane restrained prokaryotes both physically and computationally.
source: What restrained these early cells, both physically and computationally, was the location of their power plant in the cell membrane.
evidence: This is an inference about the constraints on prokaryotic evolution.

claim: If a prokaryotic cell were to enlarge, its membrane would increase as the square of its diameter, but its volume would increase as the cube.
source: Were a cell to enlarge, its membrane would increase as the square of its diameter, but its volume would increase as the cube.
evidence: This is a mathematical relationship based on geometric principles.

claim: One bacterium invaded another and took up residence in an event so improbable that it was never repeated.
source: Then occurred an event so improbable that it was never repeated (Lane, 2014). One bacterium invaded another and took up residence.
evidence: This claim about endosymbiosis is supported by a citation to Lane, 2014.

claim: The guest bacterium gradually transferred most of its genes to the host genome, retaining only key genes needed for substrate oxidation.
source: But gradually the guest transferred most of its genes to the host genome, retaining only key genes needed for substrate oxidation.
evidence: This describes the evolutionary process of endosymbiosis based on established theory.

claim: The guest bacterium became the mitochondrion.
source: The guest, having ceded its passport (most of its genome) to the host cell, became a permanent resident, an obligatory cell organelle: the mitochondrion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the origin of mitochondria.

claim: Cells powered by mitochondria could increase the host's energy capacity by up to 100,000-fold.
source: Now that the guest was a power plant with no household to support, it could multiply without limit and increase the host's energy capacity – by up to 100,000-fold.
evidence: This is a quantitative claim about the energy advantage conferred by mitochondria, likely based on Lane, 2014.

claim: Cells powered by mitochondria could balloon from 3 micrometers in diameter to 300 micrometers.
source: Cells powered by mitochondria could now balloon from 3 micrometers in diameter to 300 micrometers, 100-fold greater diameter and 10,000-fold greater volume.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cell sizes.

claim: Eukaryotes added 3,000 new gene families along with a more complex and expensive system of gene splicing.
source: These cells – eukaryotes – added 3,000 new gene families along with a more complex and expensive system of gene splicing.
evidence: This is a statement about eukaryotic genome evolution, likely based on Lane, 2014.

claim: For Paramecium, rowing through pond water is like H. sapiens swimming through molasses.
source: First, they were constrained from foraging widely by the viscosity of water. For Paramecium, rowing through pond water is like H. sapiens swimming through molasses (Purcell, 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Purcell, 1977.

claim: There was a limit to how many different proteins could coexist in a unicellular organism without hindering function.
source: Second, despite the invention of subcellular compartments by eukaryotes, there was a limit to how many different proteins could coexist without hindering function (Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2008.

claim: Unicellular organisms grew too large to communicate internally by chemical diffusion.
source: Third, they grew too large to communicate internally by chemical diffusion (which is fast over short distances but slow over long ones).
evidence: This is based on physical principles of diffusion.

claim: A multicellular animal could enlarge by orders of magnitude and overcome the viscosity of water that had restricted foraging.
source: An animal assembled from many cells could enlarge by orders of magnitude and thus overcome the viscosity of water that had restricted foraging.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of multicellularity.

claim: Multi-cellularity solved the limit on protein diversity because cells could specialize their proteins for particular functions.
source: Multi-cellularity also solved the limit on protein diversity because now cells could specialize their proteins for particular functions such as contraction (muscle cells), metabolic storage (liver cells), and so on.
evidence: This is an inference about how multicellularity overcame constraints on unicellular organisms.

claim: About 500 million years before the present, there arose from the jellyfish line a marine worm termed the urbilaterian.
source: By about 500 million years before the present, there arose from the jellyfish line a marine worm termed the urbilaterian because it was the progenitor of all subsequent bilaterally symmetrical animals, such as insects and vertebrates (Arendt et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Arendt et al., 2008.

claim: The urbilaterian is thought to resemble its closest surviving descendent, Platynereis dumerilii.
source: From this worm, thought to resemble its closest surviving descendent, Platynereis dumerilii, we inherited some key building blocks
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative biology, likely supported by Arendt et al., 2008.

claim: Humans inherited bilateral symmetry, sensors in the head, a brain in the head, and a nerve cord from the urbilaterian.
source: From this worm, thought to resemble its closest surviving descendent, Platynereis dumerilii, we inherited some key building blocks: bilateral symmetry, which was efficient for attaching legs; sensors in the head, which was efficient for detecting what is coming and where we are going; a brain in the head, which shortens the input wires; and a brain extended as a nerve cord, which places motor circuits near their effectors and shortens the output wires.
evidence: This is based on comparative evolutionary biology.

claim: Predictive regulation minimizes the frequency and size of errors and is intrinsically more efficient than homeostasis.
source: Predictive regulation, termed allostasis, minimizes the frequency and size of errors; thus it is intrinsically more efficient than homeostasis, which waits for errors to occur and then corrects them by negative feedback (Sterling, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sterling, 2012.

claim: The circadian clock was the earliest key to predictive regulation.
source: The earliest key to predictive regulation was a circadian clock.
evidence: This is an inference about the evolution of regulatory mechanisms.

claim: The central clock governs separate clocks in each tissue so that they can predict locally when to turn on.
source: The central clock governs separate clocks in each tissue so that they can predict locally when to turn on; for example, turn on liver before meals and muscle before exercise (Gerhart-Hines and Lazar, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gerhart-Hines and Lazar, 2015.

claim: The hierarchy of clocks exists in the fruit fly, so it was probably present in the urbilaterian worm.
source: This hierarchy of clocks also exists in the fruit fly, so it too was probably present in our last common ancestor, the urbilaterian worm.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative biology.

claim: Sending signals at the lowest possible rate is cheaper and conserves resources.
source: Another principle of efficient neural design was to send signals at the lowest possible rate (that is, the fewest bits per second) because it is cheaper and conserves resources.
evidence: This is an inference about neural efficiency based on information theory and energetics.

claim: The final transfer of information by a hormone takes about the same amount of energy as is provided by one molecule of ATP.
source: Moreover, the final transfer of information by a hormone (via a G protein) takes about the same amount of energy as is provided by one molecule of ATP (Sterling and Laughlin, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sterling and Laughlin, 2015.

claim: The energy needed to send a sodium current through a single membrane channel for one millisecond takes 2,000 times the energy needed for a hormone signal.
source: To allow signals to be sent at higher rates the early brain added electrical signals, but the energy needed to send a sodium current through a single membrane channel for one millisecond to create an electrical 'spike' or signal takes 2,000 times the energy needed for a hormone signal (Perge et al., 2012; Sterling and Laughlin, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Perge et al., 2012 and Sterling and Laughlin, 2015.

claim: When a behavior delivers a result better than predicted, certain neurons reward the 'choosing circuits' by secreting a pulse of dopamine.
source: Thus, when a behavior delivers a result better than predicted, certain neurons reward the 'choosing circuits' by secreting a pulse of dopamine.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of reward learning in the brain.

claim: Reward learning by dopamine is mathematically optimal.
source: This type of reward learning is mathematically optimal, and since it is present in the fruit fly, it was probably already present in the brain of our last common ancestor the urbilaterian worm.
evidence: This is based on computational theories of learning and comparative biology.

claim: Reward learning was present in the fruit fly, so it was probably present in the urbilaterian worm.
source: This type of reward learning is mathematically optimal, and since it is present in the fruit fly, it was probably already present in the brain of our last common ancestor the urbilaterian worm.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative biology.

claim: H. sapiens experience the pulse of dopamine as a pulse of satisfaction – a brief uplift in mood.
source: Reward learning emerged early as a core principle of efficient regulation, and H. sapiens took it to a whole new level partly because we experience the pulse of dopamine as a pulse of satisfaction – a brief uplift in mood.
evidence: This connects the neurochemical mechanism to subjective experience.

claim: Chimpanzees lack the imagination to harvest what they cannot see.
source: Our nearest living relative, the chimpanzee, forages for visible edibles but lacks the imagination to harvest what it cannot see.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about chimpanzee cognition.

claim: Human foragers learned that tubers concealed beneath the ground store carbohydrates that are highly nutritious if properly processed and cooked.
source: Human foragers learned that tubers concealed beneath the ground store carbohydrates that are highly nutritious if properly processed and cooked.
evidence: This is a statement about human foraging behavior.

claim: The chimpanzee ranges over about 6 km2 of forest, but a human hunter learns to hunt effectively and safely over 12,000 km2.
source: The chimpanzee ranges over about 6 km2 of forest, but a human hunter learns to hunt effectively and safely over 12,000 km2 (Kaplan and Robson, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kaplan and Robson, 2002.

claim: Human foragers collect and process roughly five-fold more calories than a chimpanzee.
source: Human foragers collect and process roughly five-fold more calories than a chimpanzee – and do so anywhere on earth.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about caloric productivity, likely based on Kaplan and Robson, 2002.

claim: Human foragers require a three-fold larger brain than chimpanzees.
source: The requirement is a three-fold larger brain that matures gradually.
evidence: This is a comparative anatomical statement.

claim: A chimpanzee has learned all it needs to know for caloric production by age five.
source: Whereas a chimpanzee has learned all it needs to know for caloric production by age five, a human forager's passage from net consumer to net producer requires 20 years.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about developmental timelines, likely based on Kaplan and Robson, 2002.

claim: A human forager's passage from net consumer to net producer requires 20 years.
source: Whereas a chimpanzee has learned all it needs to know for caloric production by age five, a human forager's passage from net consumer to net producer requires 20 years.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kaplan and Robson, 2002.

claim: Human foragers' learning curves for gathering and hunting continue rising until around age 45.
source: Moreover, its learning curves for gathering and hunting continue rising until around age 45.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kaplan and Robson, 2002 and Gurven et al., 2017.

claim: By age 45, a hunter will have quadrupled their productivity compared to their entry level.
source: By then a hunter will have quadrupled their productivity compared to their entry level.
evidence: This is a quantitative claim about productivity gains, supported by Kaplan and Robson, 2002.

claim: Cerebral cortex of H. sapiens subdivided into about 180 different areas.
source: Ultimately cerebral cortex of H. sapiens subdivided into about 180 different areas (Glasser et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Glasser et al., 2016.

claim: There are six cortical patches for recognizing faces.
source: These include large areas for early sensory processing and motor control, but also various small, narrowly specialized areas, such as six patches for recognizing faces (Tsao et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tsao et al., 2008.

claim: As we learn to read, even in adulthood, a particular area in the left hemisphere shifts from recognizing objects to recognizing written words.
source: Moreover, the areas retain considerable plasticity. For example, as we learn to read, even in adulthood, a particular area in the left hemisphere shifts from recognizing objects to recognizing written words (Nakamura et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nakamura et al., 2012.

claim: Auditory areas on the left hemisphere emphasize language, and on the right they emphasize music.
source: First, it specializes the corresponding areas in each hemisphere. For example, auditory areas on the left emphasize language, and on the right they emphasize music (Garcea et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Garcea et al., 2017.

claim: Visual and motor tracts mature by our mid-30s and slowly regress.
source: For example, visual and motor tracts mature by our mid-30s and slowly regress, but prefrontal and temporal tracts mature around age 45 and regress much later (Yeatman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yeatman et al., 2014.

claim: Prefrontal and temporal tracts mature around age 45 and regress much later.
source: For example, visual and motor tracts mature by our mid-30s and slowly regress, but prefrontal and temporal tracts mature around age 45 and regress much later (Yeatman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yeatman et al., 2014.

claim: Each child, on its way to caloric self-sufficiency at age 20, accumulates an enormous energy debt to the family.
source: So here's the math: each child, on its way to caloric self-sufficiency at age 20, accumulates an enormous energy debt to the family.
evidence: This is based on calculations from Kaplan and Robson, 2002.

claim: Partial repayment of the energy debt occurs during the 20s and 30s via calories transferred to the children, but repayment continues from ages 40 to 70 via transfers to grandchildren.
source: Partial repayment occurs during the 20s and 30s via calories transferred to the children; but that does not suffice to retire the debt, so repayment continues from ages 40 to 70 via transfers to grandchildren (Kaplan and Robson, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kaplan and Robson, 2002.

claim: Chimpanzees repay their smaller energy debt sooner and are dead at 45.
source: Chimpanzees, by the way, repay their smaller debt sooner and are dead at 45 (Blurton Jones et al., 2002; Kaplan and Robson, 2002; Kim et al., 2012; Gurven et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Blurton Jones et al., 2002; Kaplan and Robson, 2002; Kim et al., 2012; Gurven et al., 2017.

claim: A skilled artist stenciled hands on a cave wall near the southern tip of South America nine millennia ago.
source: A skilled artist stenciled hands on a cave wall near the southern tip of South America nine millennia ago
evidence: This is a statement about archaeological evidence.

claim: A musician played a bone flute in northern Europe 40 millennia ago.
source: a musician played a bone flute in northern Europe 40 millennia ago
evidence: This is a statement about archaeological evidence.

claim: Sculptors carved abstract objects and ornaments in southern Africa between 70 and 100 millennia ago.
source: sculptors carved abstract objects and ornaments in southern Africa between 70 and 100 millennia ago.
evidence: This is a statement about archaeological evidence.

claim: Paintings of similar antiquity in a Spanish cave are attributed to H. neanderthal.
source: Paintings of similar antiquity in a Spanish cave are attributed to H. neanderthal, suggesting its capacity for sacred practice (Hoffmann et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hoffmann et al., 2018.

claim: In 1769 James Watt patented the first efficient machine that used fire to perform mechanical work.
source: For roughly two million years members of the genus Homo used fire to warm a cave and roast a root. But in 1769 James Watt patented the first efficient machine that used fire to perform mechanical work.
evidence: This is a historical fact about the steam engine.

claim: The invention of Watt's steam engine coincided with the final stages of 'enclosure' that moved English peasants from their traditional common lands into cities.
source: This invention coincided with the final stages of 'enclosure' that moved English peasants from their traditional common lands into cities (Overton, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Overton, 1996.

claim: The steam engine led to the rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide that drives global warming today.
source: The steam engine also led to the rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide that drives global warming today (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 2, which shows CO2 concentration rising after 1769.

claim: The steam engine removed men, women, and children from challenging, integrated lives in the countryside to jobs that yoked them to a machine or sent them down a mine for twelve hours a day or more.
source: The steam engine removed men, women, and children from challenging, integrated lives in the countryside to jobs that yoked them to a machine or sent them down a mine for twelve hours a day or more (Engels, 1845).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Engels, 1845.

claim: Adam Smith wrote in 1776 that a man whose life is spent performing a few simple operations naturally loses the habit of exertion and generally becomes as stupid and ignorant as possible.
source: Adam Smith had anticipated the consequence, writing in the very year that his friend's machine went on line: "The man whose life is spent in performing a few simple operations has no occasion to exert his understanding or to exercise his invention in finding out expedients for difficulties which never occur. He naturally loses, therefore, the habit of such exertion and generally becomes as stupid and ignorant as it is possible for a human creature to become" (Smith, 1776).
evidence: This is a direct quote from Adam Smith, 1776.

claim: When the abundance, comfort and social isolation of modern life shrink the sources of positive surprise required by the reward circuit, the system is compelled to seek reinforcement from their intensification.
source: What happens when the abundance, comfort and social isolation of modern life shrink the sources of positive surprise required by our ancient circuit to deliver its reinforcing pulse of dopamine? According to computational theories of reward learning, the system is compelled to seek reinforcement from their intensification (Sutton and Barto, 1998).
evidence: This claim is based on computational theories cited in Sutton and Barto, 1998.

claim: When the reward system drives consumption of carbohydrate and fat far beyond metabolic need, the regulatory circuits chronically predict a need to elevate insulin.
source: But, when the reward system drives consumption of carbohydrate and fat far beyond metabolic need, the regulatory circuits chronically predict a need to elevate insulin (Kleinridders et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kleinridders et al., 2014.

claim: Insulin receptors in many tissues, including the brain, adapt by reducing their sensitivity to insulin ('insulin resistance').
source: Insulin receptors in many tissues, including the brain, adapt by reducing their sensitivity to insulin ('insulin resistance'), and this eventually causes cells to need more insulin, which evokes further resistance.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of insulin resistance.

claim: The process of insulin resistance leads finally to type 2 diabetes.
source: The process leads finally to type 2 diabetes, whose complex pattern of endocrine signaling contributes to hypertension and vascular inflammation – thus elevating cardiovascular mortality (Figure 3; American Heart Association, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3 and a citation to American Heart Association, 2017.

claim: Unbounded consumption of drugs directly release dopamine or prolong its presence at synapses.
source: Unbounded consumption of drugs (such as nicotine, alcohol, cocaine, amphetamine and opiates) easily drive the reward circuit into an addictive cycle because they directly release dopamine or prolong its presence at synapses (Keiflin and Janak, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Keiflin and Janak, 2015.

claim: Compulsive consumption of rich foods and dopamine-elevating drugs share the same circuits.
source: Investigators of addiction now recognize that compulsive consumption of rich foods and dopamine-elevating drugs share the same circuits (Murray et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Murray et al., 2014.

claim: Contemporary foragers (hunter-gatherers) are not mostly hungry.
source: Yet, contemporary foragers (hunter-gatherers) are not mostly hungry.
evidence: This is a statement about contemporary foraging societies, likely based on Kelly, 2014.

claim: Contemporary foragers employ mathematically optimal foraging strategies to satisfy their nutritional needs with relatively few hours per week.
source: Rather they employ mathematically optimal foraging strategies to satisfy their nutritional needs with relatively few hours per week, leaving considerable free time for sacred practices.
evidence: This is based on studies of foraging societies, likely Kelly, 2014.

claim: Feeding is regulated meticulously by myriad signals from gut, liver, muscle, fat, bone and brain.
source: Feeding is regulated meticulously by myriad signals from gut, liver, muscle, fat, bone and brain (Garfield et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Garfield et al., 2015.

claim: Animals in the wild, including H. sapiens, tend neither to overeat nor over-forage.
source: Consequently animals in the wild, including H. sapiens, tend neither to overeat nor over-forage.
evidence: This is a general statement about animal behavior in natural environments.

claim: Essentially all human populations across the planet are rapidly depositing fat.
source: Now, except for regions of periodic famine and warfare, essentially all human populations across the planet – whatever their genotype – are rapidly depositing fat (GBD 2015 Obesity Collaborators et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to GBD 2015 Obesity Collaborators et al., 2017.

claim: Fruit fly larvae fed a high-carbohydrate diet develop hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes and high plasma levels of triglycerides and free fatty acids.
source: Moreover, fruit fly larvae fed a high-carbohydrate diet also develop hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes and high plasma levels of triglycerides and free fatty acids (Musselman et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Musselman et al., 2011.

claim: Human mechanisms of metabolic regulation were apparently inherited from the urbilaterian ancestor.
source: Thus human mechanisms of metabolic regulation were apparently inherited from our shared urbilaterian ancestor, suggesting that all animals are vulnerable to obesity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of metabolic mechanisms across species.

claim: Obesity is highest in countries with greatest inequality of income, with the United States literally taking the cake.
source: This may explain why obesity is highest in countries with greatest inequality of income, with the United States literally taking the cake (Wilkinson and Pickett, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wilkinson and Pickett, 2010.

claim: Within the United States, obesity is highest in the most unequal states, and highest among the least educated.
source: And within the United States, obesity is highest in the most unequal states, and highest among the least educated (Ogden, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ogden, 2010.

claim: The resemblance of binge eating to opioid addiction suggests an antagonist of the µ opioid receptor as a therapeutic agent.
source: For example, the resemblance of binge eating to opioid addiction suggests an antagonist of the µ opioid receptor as a therapeutic agent (Ziauddeen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ziauddeen et al., 2013.

claim: By age eighteen nearly 50% of US boys have systolic pressures of 130 mm Hg or higher.
source: By age eighteen nearly 50% of US boys have systolic pressures of 130 mm Hg or higher (Falkner, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Falkner, 2005.

claim: The brain regularly predicts a need for higher blood pressure and drives all components of the blood pressure regulation circuit.
source: The brain, regularly predicting a need for higher pressure, drives all components of the circuit (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 4.

claim: Figure 1 shows the brain's fundamental challenge is to match the inner needs of metabolism and physiology with the outer needs of behavior.
source: Figure 1.
evidence: Figure 1 illustrates the brain's core tasks in predictive regulation.
